title: Connectors and MCP servers
trust_boundary: Before: the model sees what the user pastes. After: it reads from and writes to other systems through tools whose names, descriptions and results are supplied by whoever runs the server.
Tool descriptions and tool results enter the context as text the model cannot authenticate. A server can change its tool list after it was approved.
The connector holds credentials (OAuth tokens, API keys) and acts with a user's or a service account's permissions.
With several connectors enabled, data read through one can be sent out through another.
context_questions: Which connectors and servers, run by whom: the model vendor, the system's own vendor, a third party, yourselves?
Read-only or read-write? Acting as the user or as a shared service account?
Who may add a new connector: an administrator, or any user?

threats.title: Tool poisoning: instructions hidden in tool descriptions
threats.description: A tool's metadata tells the model to do something the user never asked for. Nothing has to be called for the text to take effect.
questions: Who wrote each tool description, and has anyone read them?
Does the client show descriptions to the user or an administrator, and flag changes?
How does the model behave when a description contains instructions?
vendor_evidence: Model or client testing against poisoned tool metadata.
Review or signing of connectors in the vendor's directory.

own_tests.how: its extension kind measures how well a scanner of MCP servers and skills detects bad ones. It evaluates the scanner, not your servers; scanning itself is outside this repo.

no_standard_test: The servers you will actually connect. Public sets use their own server collections.

threats.title: Injection through what a tool returns
threats.description: A ticket, email, document or record fetched by a connector carries instructions, and the agent follows them.
questions: Which connectors return content that outsiders can write: inboxes, issue trackers, shared drives, web search?
Is tool output marked as data when it reaches the model?
What can the agent do next if it is hijacked: which write actions are in reach?
vendor_evidence: Published injection results for tool use: benchmark, attack type, safeguards on or off.
A description of safeguards on tool output.

own_tests.how: adaptive attacks against your own endpoint, if the connectors sit behind one.
a fixed set of attack and benign prompts against the same endpoint.

no_standard_test: Your own connectors, data and permissions.

threats.title: A malicious, compromised or changed server
threats.description: The server itself is hostile: published to be installed, taken over later, renamed to collide with a trusted one, or changed after approval.
questions: Where does each server come from, and who vets it before it is enabled?
Is the version pinned? Is anyone told when the tool list or a description changes?
Can two servers offer a tool with the same name, and which one wins?
vendor_evidence: How the vendor's directory reviews connectors.
Client behaviour on changed tool definitions.

own_tests.how: extension kind, as under mcp-01: it tells you how far to trust a scanner.

no_standard_test: Change over time. No benchmark watches a server you depend on.

threats.title: Over-broad permissions and credential handling
threats.description: The connector's token can do more than the task needs, is stored where it can be read, or lets one user act with another's rights.
questions: What scopes does each token carry, and are they the narrowest the system offers?
Where are tokens stored, and can the model or a tool read them?
Does the connector act as the asking user, with that user's permissions, every time?
vendor_evidence: The authorisation model of each connector.
no_standard_test: Design review of scopes and identities. No benchmark.

threats.title: Data read through one tool leaves through another
threats.description: Private content fetched by one connector is written, sent or encoded into a call to another that an attacker can read.
questions: Which enabled tools can send data outside: email, web requests, posting, file sharing?
Can a session hold private data and an outbound tool at the same time?
Are tool calls and their arguments logged?
vendor_evidence: Exfiltration results in the vendor's tool-use testing.

own_tests.how: against your own endpoint, with canary data you plant.

no_standard_test: The particular combination of connectors you enable.

threats.title: Destructive or unintended writes through tools
threats.description: The agent deletes, overwrites, sends or changes something in a connected system, by error or under manipulation.
questions: Which tools write, and which writes cannot be undone?
Which calls need a person's approval, and what does the approval show?

threats.title: The server or its transport is itself exposed
threats.description: A server reachable without authentication, a local server that runs commands with the user's rights, or a server that can be made to fetch internal addresses.
questions: Is each remote server authenticated, and to whom is it reachable?
Do local servers run commands or read files with the user's privileges?
vendor_evidence: Security documentation or audit of each server.
no_standard_test: Conventional security review of the server. Outside what an AI benchmark measures.
